title: The Last Alibi Again
premise: Estate lawyer Wren Reyes is summoned to probate a will for a man who died two years ago — and the document names her as executor, though she never met him. Twin letters arrive with the file: one confessing to a murder the courts already closed, one promising that 'the ledger remembers what the family buried.' As Wren decodes a household account book whose entries are really confessions, she discovers the victim was her own estranged father's business partner, and the found family that took her in as a teen may have built itself on a covered-up death. At the anniversary dinner where the killer plans to confess publicly or silence Wren permanently, she reads the final ledger entry aloud, forcing justice outside the courtroom — and chooses the makeshift family she's rebuilt over the blood ties that failed her.
about_author: Vesper Crane spent a decade clerking for probate courts before trading the bar for fiction, and their mysteries are known for legal procedural texture braided with quiet emotional devastation. They live in a coastal town full of old houses and older secrets, which they insist is coincidence.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Opening a routine probate, Wren finds a will dated after its maker's death, naming her executor of an estate she has no connection to. Attached: two letters, one a murder confession, one addressed only to 'the one who keeps the books.' The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into personal dread when she recognizes her own childhood address in the estate inventory.

chapters.title: Entries in Red Ink
chapters.summary: Alternating Wren's POV with ledger excerpts. Wren obtains the household account book and realizes mundane purchases encode dates, initials, and payments — hush money spanning fifteen years. A threatening call warns her off before the anniversary dinner. The beat deepens from curiosity to complicity-adjacent fear as she recognizes the handwriting: it belongs to Marisol, the woman who fostered her.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, single continuous evening. She attends the dinner under pretext, ledger hidden in her bag, while the family performs grief for a man they killed twice — once in body, once in memory. When the patriarch proposes a toast, Wren stands instead and begins reading the decoded entries aloud. Climactic beat: betrayal, exposed truths, and Marisol's tearful admission that the cover-up protected Wren herself.

chapters.title: What the Books Keep
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, weeks later. Rather than hand everything to police, Wren brokers restitution through the estate she now controls, funding the victim's forgotten daughter and dissolving the family's holdings. Marisol turns herself in; Wren visits her, forgiveness unfinished but real. Final beat: belonging redefined — Wren hosts her own first dinner, setting a place for the daughter, closing the ledger for good.
